utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the Registrar would call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-PT the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Geoffrey Nice with Ken Scott on my right, Rod Dixon on my left and Ms. Verhaag the case manager for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Turner Smith, Your Honour, for the defendant Dario Kordic, with Dr. Turkovic on my left, and then my colleague David Geneson and our co-counsel Mitko Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) good morning, Your Honour. Appearance for Cerkez Defence is the same, Bozidar Kovacic, attorney from Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: May I be assured that the accused can hear the proceedings a language which they understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you for your interest as to whether we understand the proceedings. Yes, we do understand in Croatian what is going on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I understand, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, this hearing has been listed to consider various motions which have been entered, and as we came in, we were given a proposed schedule. I don't know whose handiwork it is. I expect Mr. Smith, although I don't know. I think we had probably intended to follow the programme as it's set out here. Have you got a copy of this, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I would have thought, in fact, it might be easier to deal with all the jurisdictional motions together, if the argument could be organised in that way, with the Defence presenting their argument in relation to all of them, Prosecutor replying, and then we would move on to the form of the indictment, and again, follow that proposed course of action with both sides presenting all their argument together. I see that in some cases that there will be no argument. The only matter which is of concern is about the time, and that is that very little time is being left, according to this programme, to deal with the motion about compliance which has been left to the last, and that seems, to me, to be an important matter because it deals with the whole question of disclosure. What I propose that we do when it comes to that motion, is that we review the position as it is today about disclosure, and then move on from there to decide what can be done, and then decide what issues there are for the Trial Chamber to resolve on disclosure. We'll begin with jurisdiction, and, Mr. Smith, if you're going to address us first, I think we would find it helpful to hear all the argument on jurisdiction together on your various points, and then we'll hear from the Prosecution. Bear in mind, of course, that we have read the motions. They are fairly voluminous, so we are very much au fait with the argument. I would be grateful if people would not repeat what's already said. There is a motion before the Chamber which was filed, I think, yesterday, applying for more -- for leave, rather, on behalf of the defence to file a reply in support of jurisdictional motion number 2. Unless the Prosecution wish to make any sort of objection to that, it may be convenient for us to say that we are prepared to grant leave and we've read the motion -- or, rather, the brief, I should say. Mr. Smith, then we'll hear you first on the jurisdiction point and then hear anybody else for the Defence and then call on the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, with leave might I request that I address jurisdictional motion number 2 for ten minutes and Dr. Turkovic address jurisdictional motion number 3 for five minutes, and each of us reserve five minutes for reply argument at the end of a total of 25 minutes of argument by the Prosecution on both motions. I'm perfectly happy to argue both at the same time. We're have prepared each to argue different motions on our side. If, howeve you need them all argued by one counsel that can be accommodated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sure that's not necessary. Do it in whatever order you would, but let's hear all your arguments first on jurisdiction and then we'll hear the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you, Your Honour. We are indeed resting on briefs -- on jurisdictional motion number 1 and 4, that obviously belies no lack of confidence in the arguments we've raised there, but there's an extremely limited amount of time for some very complex arguments on a large number of them, and we will felt it essential to pick and choose which briefs we thought most would benefit, and where the Trial Chamber would most benefit from oral argument and as a result have chosen jurisdictional motions 2 and 3. If I may then start on jurisdictional motion 2. As Your Honours will know, we are arguing that, first, the Laws and Customs of War under Article 3, that language in the Statute are limited to offences under its express provisions and under those in the 1907 Hague Convention and its regulations on which Article 3 was based. Article 3 does not cover, in our judgment, Common Article 3 and the protocols of the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The remedy we are suggesting then is that the counts listed in our motion be stricken, or alternatively, that all references to the Geneva Convention and protocols in those counts be stricken. We believe this is a question solely of law and thus can and must be decided now prior to trial. Articles 2 and 3, our second argument, are, in our judgment, limited to offences committed within the context of an international armed conflict. The scope of Articles 2 and 3 in this regard is also, in our judgment, a question of law. That should be resolved prior to trial. Distinct from the application of that scope to the facts in determining whether, in fact, there is or is not an international armed conflict, we're arguing here the scope issue. The remedy, again, is striking the counts outlined in our motion on the grounds that there is no international armed conflict and no armed conflict at all between Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat communities in the Lasva Valley region during much of the period covered by the indictment, this remedy to be granted now or the at such time as the Trial Chamber later determines during or after trial upon examination of the facts. Let me then turn to the argument. Article 1 of the Statute gives the Tribunal power to prosecute "In accordance with the provisions of the present Statute." And the Secretary-General, in his report states that under the principle of nullem crimen sine lege, the Tribunal should only apply rules which are "Beyond any doubt part of customary law." These, Your Honour, are the linchpins of our argument. Given these two clearly applicable premises, we believe that the decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic case is in serious fundamental and widely acknowledged error for the reasons that we set out in detail in our brief and in our reply brief. In particular, its error lies in, number one, concluding that Article 3 includes all violations of International Humanitarian Law, not otherwise covered by Articles 2, 4 and 5. Secondly, that it is in error in -- because of its unfounded conclusion, that it "Does not matter whether the serious violation has occurred within the context of an international or an internal armed conflict." Tadic does, however, in our judgment, correctly conclude that the scope of Article 2 is limited to situations involving international armed conflict. The first issue I want to address, Your Honours, is that this Trial Chamber is free to decide the Article 3 issue. The Prosecutor has said, as you will know, that the Tadic Appeal Chamber decision is legally binding on the Trial Chamber. This, in our judgment, is not so. First, International Law courts are not generally bound by precedents. Decisions are considered for their persuasive effect but are not legally binding. Second, nothing in the Tribunal's Statute or in its Regulations indicates that there should be a binding effect to Appeals Chamber decisions. Third, the question whether the Appeal Chamber decisions are legally binding on Trial Chambers, other than the Trial Chamber in that case, is a question that has not been resolved by the Appeals Chamber itself. Next, the Trial Chambers cited by the Prosecutor as having respected or being bound, as they say, by the appellant decision in Tadic, have not, in fact, themselves, when you examine the opinions as we do in our reply brief, consider themselves bound. They have re-examined the decision. Next, the Tribunal deals with complex and sophisticated issues, many of them of first impression and affecting individual liberty. The law on these issues should not be prematurely frozen. Next, each defendant has a right to full and fair hearing on the law, and this argues strongly against finding the Tadic Appeal Chamber decision binding legally. Next, the importance of the issues raised by the Defence in this motion and the significance of the errors committed, as we believe we have demonstrated by the Tadic appeal decision, argues strongly in favour of this Trial Chamber refusing to follow that ruling. Finally, the interests in judicial economy are adequately protected, we believe, by the normal rule of considering the persuasive effect of a prior decision even by a higher tribunal in the international context. In short, this Trial Chamber is, in our judgment, free and should feel free to consider our arguments and re-examine the conclusions in Tadic in light of the arguments we have made, many of which we think are beyond the arguments made previously, and in any case, go to the reasoning of the Tadic decision, demonstrating why we believe the reasoning is fallacious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Smith, consider the practicalities of this submission of yours. It means, doesn't it, that there would be no finality in much of the work of the Tribunal, because if you're right and every Trial Chamber can consider every question afresh, it means that litigation could never be brought to an end. It also means that there isn't any certainty for those who practice here and those who are tried here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may suggest, I believe that the rule of a persuasive effect, properly applied as it is in international tribunals, would lead to reasonable certainty. Over time as more cases come through, people will develop a feel for where the Trial Chambers are coming out and the appeals -- where the Appeals Chamber is insisting, and a flexibility in the early stages of the consideration of the very complicated and very significant issues now being raised really in litigation in many ways for the first time since World War II, these need to be fully fleshed out and fully argued in the early years of the Tribunal's existence. And I think there will be certainty, reasonable certainty, because Trial Chambers are not lightly going to disregard the reasoning of the Appeals Chamber or of other Trial Chambers, but the ability to do so, at least until the Appeals Chamber has spoken to the contrary, seems, to me, to be essential to the operation of the Tribunal's justice system at this early stage. I have about used, I think, the ten minutes, and if we are going to stay on schedule, as we must, if we are going to end up able to argue all of the motions we would like to, I will rest on brief as to the main points in the argument saying only that we believe we have demonstrated across the board and in depth the difficulty and the illogic of the Appeals Chamber's Tadic decision. We believe these issues are very serious because they import wholesale into Article 3 all the rest of International Humanitarian Law and make it applicable as individual criminal liability against defendants. We do not believe that that squares with the language which refers to language from the 1907 convention. We do not believe that it is consistent with the intent of the Security Council, and we urge Your Honours to look at the Celebeci opinions discussion of the necessity for construing criminal statues narrowly. And in favour of the defendant -- ambiguity and given the barrage of criticism of the Appellant Chamber's decision here, we think it's undeniable that there's ambiguity in Article 3 on this matter. Thank you, Your Honour, and Dr. Turkovic will address jurisdictional motion number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Bennouna would like to raise a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I am going to speak in French. Can you hear me? It is simply to, I think, assist the Tribunal, as you yourself have proposed, to have a clearer idea of the jurisdiction, which is very essential, as you have said, and we must make progress in that area, and regarding which both the doctrine and the practice, internationally, is watching over what is happening here. You told us that the basis is Article 1 regarding the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, which says that the Tribunal has the jurisdiction to try persons committing serious offences on the territory of ex-Yugoslavia since 1991. And you have added to the preparatory work the quotation from the Secretary-General of the U.N. regarding the principle of equality, and the principle of nullum crimen sine lege. Mr. Smith, would you agree that through Article 1 and the preparatory work, this Tribunal is applying not only the statute,and conventional law but also international customary law?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would articulate it this way.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I would articulate it this way: That the Tribunal is applying the language of this Tribunal Statute, Article 1, which refers it then to the language of Articles 2, 3, 4 and 5. And it is limited in its application and interpretation of the language of the Statute, referring now to "in accordance with the provisions of the present Statute," in Article 1, it is limited in its reading of the language of the charging Articles, 2, 3, 4 and 5, to the customary international law in effect, we believe, at the time that the offences were committed or the alleged offences were committed. In any case, in effect the time the Statute was created. Does that answer Your Honours question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Not quite. You say that Article 1 refers also to Articles 2, 3, 5 and so on, and it also refers to international customary law as it existed at the time the Statute was adopted. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On the latter point, the limitation to customary law as it existed at the time of the offence, I am referring to the language in the Secretary-General's report, which states that it is the intent of the Security Council that when the Tribunal applies the International Humanitarian Law which is embodied in the language of Articles 2, 3 and 5, it is limited in so doing to only applying that which was customary international law at the time we believe when the alleged offences were committed. Have I now succeeded in making myself clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) This is what I have understand from this clarification you have made. At the time the offence was committed, the Tribunal is authorised to apply positive international law as regards the statutory provisions, and also international customary law, such as it existed, at the time the offences were committed. Is that so? Because the Statute refers to international customary law. This is a very important question and, in any event, I wanted you to confirm this. But I was going to say that this is only natural, because as an international tribunal we are bound by international customary law and by rules that are applied even beyond international rules and the Statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I am saying, I believe, is that Your Honour is, as you say, bound by and limited by customary international law, but you are also bound initially by the language of the Statute that creates the Tribunal, so that to the extent that that language incorporates customary international law, or is derived from the Geneva Convention in terms of Article 2 or the 1907 Hague Convention in terms of Article 3, to that extent this Tribunal is authorised to apply customary international law. If the question is would the Tribunal be authorised to apply customary international law in the abstract, even if, let's assume for purposes of argument, it could find no statutory basis in Articles 2, 3 or 5, I think I would argue no. You are bound initially by the Statute which created the Tribunal and by its language, but that that Statute incorporates deliberately and by the drafters provisions from the Geneva Convention from the 1907 Hague Convention. It is fashioned on them. That's, I think, my argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will address jurisdictional motion number 3. In her reply brief to jurisdictional number 3, the Prosecutor did not advance any argument to rebut the Defence position that mere planning and preparation should not be punishable under the Statute. Mere planning and preparation meaning planning and preparation when the crime has not been afterwards completed or at least attempted. Instead, the Prosecutor completely confused two concepts existing in criminal law. They are complicity, which refers to ways in which persons may participate in the commission of the offence, the roles that parties to the crime may assume, and that of preparation, which is one of the stages in the commission of the crime. Throughout her reply brief the Prosecutor is talking about complicity, more precisely, about aiding and abetting, and even more precisely, about aiding and abetting accomplished through prepatory acts when the offence occurred thereafter. The Defence does not deny and is actually fully agreeing with the Prosecutor's assertions that aiding and abetting, when it is performed in the form of prepatory acts, is punishable, if other prerequisites are fulfilled, prerequisites such as mental state, completion of the offence or attempt of the offence and others that we will discuss during the main trial, because this is the initial interpretation. In its jurisdictional motion number 3, the Defence was only arguing that mere planning and preparation of crimes listed in the Tribunal Statute is neither punishable according to customary law nor according to general principles of law, nor according to the criminal law of former Yugoslavia. I have a little handout. It would be easier to follow what I will argue. If we can just give that to the people, I believe. Thank you for the assistance. Your Honours, the Defence would like to draw your attention to the parts of the indictment where the Prosecutor has charged the defendants not only with aiding and abetting accomplished through prepatory acts, but is charging them with planning and preparation which is not connected to the completed offence. Bear in mind that Prosecutor is alleging in her reply brief that she is charging the defendants only with participating in the planning and preparation of the offences that have occurred thereafter. What you do have in front of you is the language that is coming from the indictment, and it says in Count 1, paragraph 36, that is what you have in front of you, third line says, "Dario Kordic caused, planned, instigated, ordered or committed, or aided and abetted the planning, preparation or execution of a crime." This language necessarily means that each of these elements, causing, planning and so on, is independent and that the Prosecutor is charging the defendants with causing a crime, planning a crime, instigating a crime, ordering a crime, committing a crime, aiding and abetting a crime. The very same language the Prosecutor uses in all Counts of the indictment. First of all, the Defence would like to say that it is utterly surprised that even after amending the indictment the Prosecutor is still charging causing a crime. There are no grounds whatsoever what responsibility for mere causation. This is strict liability standard, which is completely in odds with mens rea requirement and standards of liability in criminal law. Now, let's go to the planning language, the third sentence that you have. Dario Kordic planned a crime. Let us concentrate for a moment on that. It is obvious because of the use of comma and connection "or" before the word "aiding and abetting" that the Prosecutor is charging the defendants for planning, regardless whether the offence was afterwards completed or not. This permits charging planning as mere preparation and, as the Defence has demonstrated in its jurisdictional motion number 3, this is contrary to customary international criminal law. This is contrary to general principles of criminal law. And this is contrary to the criminal law as existed in former Yugoslavia or as it exist in the countries that became to existence after the dissolution of the country. The Prosecutor asserts in reply brief that in the present case the accused are charged with participating in the planning and preparation of offence that occurred thereafter. Sorry. This assertion does not cure the fact that Defence is complaining about. First, the Defence will not know whether the Prosecutor charged the defendant for preparation only of completed offence until the Prosecutor will put all the evidence in. How can we know that? And it is obvious that the language on the indictment simply does not do what the Prosecutor says. It does. Thus, the word "planning" should be stricken. There is a second use of the word "planning and preparation." This is the fourth that you have on that list. Notice that the connection "or" is used before the word "execution," thus the defendants are actually charged with aiding and abetting and planning, aiding and abetting and preparation, aiding and abetting and execution. The first two, if there is no completed offence, or at least attempted offence, are contrary, as we have already said, to customary law, criminal customary law, general principles of criminal law and criminal law as existed in former Yugoslavia or as it is today. The Prosecutor should be allowed to charge only the third, the aiding and abetting in execution of a crime. The words "planning and preparation" should be stricken out. By striking these words, the Prosecutor will be still able to charge what she is claiming that she is charging in the present indictment, and that is aiding and abetting performed through prepatory acts which contribute to execution of a crime. The Prosecutor will not be able to charge the defendants with aiding and abetting and planning or preparation when the offence thereafter was not completed or at least was not attempted. The result that we have now is completely illogical, the result that we have in the indictment. To allow Prosecutor to charge for aiding and abetting and planning, if planning per se cannot be charged is illogical, because the accomplice then is liable. We know in theory the accomplice is liable in theory only if principle offence has been committed or attempted. And here we don't have principle offence. To allow Prosecutor to charge for aiding and abetting in preparation is even more illogical because even in a present indictment preparation per se has not been charged.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. To summarise, the defence respectfully request the words "causing, planning, and planning and preparation" to be stricken all the Counts of the indictment and then the language in the indictment will read -- this is the last thing that you see -- "instigated, ordered, or committed or aided and abetted execution of a crime." This way the indictment will charge what the Prosecutor is claiming in his or her response brief to jurisdictional motion number 3 that the indictment is charging now, but actually it's not, and the indictment will be logical and in accordance with the principles of criminal law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the basis for saying that under customary international law, planning an offence is not an offence?

utterances.speaker: MS. TURKOVIC
utterances.text: If you have read the -- and I suppose you did, as you did read the response brief by the prosecutors, you could find there on several places that they claim that planning and preparation was actually punishable during the Second World War. If you like, I have another handout where I can show that actually that is not the truth. If I can find it; just a second. Is there someone to hand that out, so that we can see what actually is going on? You see, if you look at the handout from the Nuremberg charter, then you would see -- and I have underlined for you -- "crimes against peace," and that it was enacted that planning and preparation of a war of aggression is criminalalised, can be punished. You don't find that language either in war crimes or in crimes against humanity. So this language of planning and preparation is language of punishing, planning, and preparation per se. And it exists just in crimes against peace. Further on, you have this last paragraph, which is actually talking not about mere preparation and planning, but is introducing the conspiracy into the Nuremberg charter, and it was decided during the trials then -- and the Prosecutor acknowledges that in his reply brief -- that conspiracy referred only to crimes against peace. The Prosecutor is giving several examples where he's citing the language of, presumably, preparation in his response brief, and is telling that because of that language, the Tribunal in fact was punishing for preparatory acts. I must say that I was really very happy when I saw their response in the response brief, because I'm glad that we agree that acts that they cite are preparatory acts. And I would say -- you know, it's very difficult to draw the line between what is preparatory act and what is substantive steps over the commission of the offence. Obviously the judges during the Second -- that they were judging the Second World War crimes thought that acts were cited that were not preparatory acts but substantive steps. To me they seem as preparatory acts the same as they seem to the prosecutors. However, you see, at that time they were thought to be substantive steps toward the commission of the crime, and that's why they were punished. If you look at the ICC statute, you do not find the language of planning or preparation there. If you look in the national laws of many countries, you would not find such language, that preparation or planning is punishable per se. You can even find countries in which it is expressly prohibited to punish for preparation and planning per se. Why is that so? Because for a long time that was punishable, like 50 years ago; it's the same as, for example, in the 18th Century, when they decided they will want punish for mere thoughts, some criminal statutes had express prohibition of punishing for mere thoughts, because it was punished for such a long time. So you see, this is something that we have in criminal law for the past 50 years, and it was already acknowledged during the trials, Nuremberg trials, that we cannot punish for mere preparation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does anybody else want to say anything for the Defence? Very well, we'll call on the Prosecution. If you could take the matter as briefly as possible, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Dixon will deal with the first motion, and I'll deal with the second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, in response to the Defence contention that only the 1907 Hague regulations are included in Article 3, we, the Prosecutors, submit that it is well-established that since 1907, the body of international humanitarian law has expanded considerably. There were the Geneva Conventions of 1929 passed thereafter; it is also well known that in 1949, further Geneva Conventions were passed, and that within those conventions which were applicable to only international armed conflicts, there was a provision, Article 3, common to all of the conventions, which is also applicable to noninternational armed conflict. It is accepted that the rules contained in Common Article 3 apply to all conflicts. The International Court of Justice has declared that these prohibitions represent elementary considerations of humanity which apply to all conflicts, irrespective of whether those are international or internal. After the Geneva Conventions in 1977, two protocols additional to those conventions were passed, one applicable to international armed conflict and the other, additional protocol 2, applicable to internal armed conflicts. The Prosecutor submits that all of these rules of international humanitarian law are covered under the laws and customs of war as provided for in Article 3 of the statute. So not only the rules of 1907. The only exception is the grave breach provisions of the 1949 Geneva Conventions, which the Tribunal is specifically empowered to prosecute under Article 2 of the statute. The basis for this is threefold, in the Prosecutor's view. Firstly, the Tribunal is mandated to prosecute all serious violations of international humanitarian law; that's in terms of Article 1 of the statute. And the Tribunal can give effect to this mandate by incorporating all serious violations of international humanitarian law within Article 3. Secondly, the wording of Article 3 refers to the laws and customs of war, and the list is not exhaustive. It reads "including but not limited to" the acts that are listed thereunder. Thirdly, statements by prominent members of the Security Council, when the statute was passed and after the statute was passed, show that it was the intention of the Security Council to include more than simply the provisions that were listed in the statute. And they specifically mentioned Common Article 3, and treaties and agreements that were binding on the parties to the conflict. In addition, the Appeals Chamber of the Tribunal has held that Article 3 does include all serious violations of international humanitarian law, and this decision has been followed by Trial Chambers before the Yugoslavia Tribunal and before the Rwanda Tribunal. And we would invite Your Honours to follow the decision of the Appeals Chamber, and wish to submit that if one of the main functions of the Appeals Chamber is to ensure consistency and certainty and finality on the same issues, with respect to the jurisprudence and the practice of the Tribunals, that this can only be achieved through the Tribunal giving precedential effect to the decisions of the Appeals Chamber. The Appeals Chamber held that Common Article 3 and the provisions concerning attacks in additional protocol 1 and 2, those considering unlawful attacks on civilians and civilian objects, these are the particular provisions that are charged in the current indictment. The Appeals Chamber held that those provisions are specifically included in Article 3 of our statute, because they are part of customary international law for both conflicts at the time that the offences were committed, and also they attract individual criminal responsibility. And in any event, those treaties are binding on the parties in the former Yugoslavia. So for these reasons, we submit that the Defence's motion should be rejected and that the charges that are brought under Article 3 of the statute in the indictment should remain as such. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to jurisdictional motion 3, the motion on planning, we argue that it is well-established as an element of international humanitarian law already. We cite authority. But the Court will know that at Nuremberg, the charter did not specifically refer to planning, although there were convictions in respect of those involved in planning, albeit of completed offences. And the Tribunal will know further that the control council law number 10, the charter for the American tribunal for subsequent trials and the French Penal Code dealing with subsequent trials to which we refer made specific allowance for planning, either using that word or associated or similar words. Our statute sets out quite specifically the very terms that have been used in charging these defendants. And the Tribunal will know that Trial Chambers both here and in Rwanda -- which of course have only persuasive significance -- but nevertheless the Chamber should know that they have indicated the wide range of potential fact situations covered by this Article, paragraph 8 of our response. The position is that the opening clause of Article 7(1) describes a wide range of potential involvements, any of which in the alternative would be sufficient. And there is no reason at this stage not to leave the indictment exactly the way that it is, it ultimately being, of course, as always, a mixed question of fact and law which if any allegations are made good to the usual high standard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, in reply, a great majority of the points made by the Prosecutor on argument are already dealt with at some length in our brief. I will pick only several to respond to and to discuss. First, regarding the persuasive effect of the Tadic opinion, I would note that the Prosecutor has said in their brief that that decision was a unanimous decision, but in fact there's a dissent by Judge Lee on both of the issues we raise. And he dissents on both of them, although he finds an international armed conflict. We refer to this at page 25 of our brief. Second, as to the Security Council statements, they are of course post hoc. And as indicated in our brief and by commentators, there was no one that could have objected, the way the matter came up at the time. The two decisions cited by the Prosecutor, I urge you to look at carefully: The Corfu decision and the Namibia decision. Neither one of those, in our judgment, stands for the proposition asserted that the post hoc legislative history of a Security Council resolution is persuasive or should be considered. The Corfu decision is an entirely different context, dealing with letters, accepting jurisdiction by the countries involved in litigation. The Namibia case says nothing about resolutions or language after the Security Council has acted, but instead speaks only in general terms about aids to interpretation, and speaks about language before adoption. Finally, on the question of the Yugoslav treaties, Your Honour, I would direct your attention to page 39 of our opening brief, where we deal with the question of whether there are Yugoslavia treaties binding in this situation. And we offer three reasons why there are not, the most compelling of which, in my judgment, is that the matters brought in to Yugoslav law, protocol 2, protocol 1, the Geneva Conventions, are not self-executing, and are not made binding on individuals under Yugoslav law. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TURKOVIC
utterances.text: If I could maybe explain this past point, explain since I'm coming from former Yugoslavia. So this is maybe more clear to me then to the people that operate here. You see, the constitution of former Yugoslavia, the treaties can be applied directly, but of course to apply the treaty directly it has to be self-executing. In the Protocol 1, Protocol 2, Geneva Conventions, self-executive are only grave breaches. So whatever you find in these treaties could be applied in Yugoslavia only if a special provision in criminal code has been provided. That's it. Let me address the issues that have been raised in connectin to--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We ask counsel to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TURKOVIC
utterances.text: The issues that have been raised in connection with jurisdictional motion number 3, we have already addressed the issue of the Nuremberg Charter, and I would just like to add the language that is cited by the Prosecutor is the language of certain acts that could be preparatory acts and not necessarily need be preparatory acts, the language from the Nuremberg court. In Nuremberg, tribunals never said that these acts they cited are preparatory acts and that they are punishing for preparatory acts. They specifically said that preparatory acts can be punished only in connection with the crimes against peace. So the only conclusion that we can draw from that, knowing criminal law, is that they were considered to present -- represent a substantive step towards the commission of the crime and that's why these examples that they have given were punished the at that time. Now, as regarding the control council number -- council law number 10, again, in these control council law number 10, Article 2, paragraph 1 states specifically that planning and preparation of a crime against peace can be punished only if it is done as a crime against peace. Article 2 paragraph 2 though, says that it is possible to punish for acts that were connected with plans or enterprises involving its commission. So from that you can infer that according to control council law number 2, maybe planning was punishable, but enterprises involving its commission that doesn't say that is preparation. Furthermore, these decisions, control council law number 10, were heavily criticised after that, and it was said that they are contradicting basic principles of criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. TURKOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. And you can find that and read that in Basione's treatise. Furthermore, it was by -- it was in cases cited, and this is justice case Judge Blair cited and said that these cases that were decided according to control council law number 10, did not purport to establish by legislative act any new crimes of international applicability, and if you read literature you will find that this control council law number 10 is considered to not constitute a valid international precedent because it was considered as a national court of Germany, not international court that was deciding upon these cases. Then French, the Prosecutor is citing Aritcle 60 of the French old Court Penal. I must say they start to cite from the middle of the sentence omitting the beginning of the sentence and the beginning of the sentence is really important. The beginning says, "Has wittingly aided or assisted the author or authors of the crime or offence in any act preparatory to," and so on. So what is this Article talking about? It's talking about complicity. It's not talking about mere preparation and mere planning. So this is, again, not a good example. Then they're giving the example from the law reports of the trials of war criminals, volume 15, page 49. The title of the whole section is "Rules Relating to the Complicity". So whatever is stated there is related to complicity. It's not related to mere preparation or to mere planning as a preparatory act. I already said that the ICC Statute you cannot find that language. At the beginning it was there under the influence of the language that we find in the present Statute, but then it was taken out because it was seen that actually doesn't make sense and that it is not in accordance with principles of criminal law. This language from Article 7, it is indeed the same as the language in the indictment, but that doesn't mean that this language is not in contradiction to what we find in customary law, what we find in criminal law. This language actually is completely illogical. As I have shown to you, there is nothing that says that mere preparation is penalised in this language. Nothing. But it says that aiding and abetting in preparation is penalised. How that could be? This is contrary to everything you find in criminal law. Unfortunately, it seems to the Defence that too often this Statute was drafted by people who were real great experts in International Humanitarian Law but sometimes lacked enough knowledge of criminal law, so sometimes we are getting bad results if we are watching that from the perspective of the criminal law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Bennouna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I have a question for Madam Turkovic. First of all, I note that there is a certain contradiction with what Mr. Smith said a moment ago, because you're telling us that regardless of the provisions of the Statute, we should go back to customary law. That is what I understand from your statement. So Article 7 should be read in the light of customary law, and that the whole Statute should be read in the light of customary law. My question is as follows -- you say that those who drafted the statue are not sufficiently familiar with criminal law. My question is: Don't you think that there is a specific aspect of the international humanitarian law within criminal law or penal law, and that normally, and that there is a great specificity when we talk about crimes against peace and security of mankind, and is that not the reason that we talk about planning, instigating, commission, et cetera, of that type of crimes, which, as you know, are crimes committed on a large scale and which require certain means which are not the same means used as in regular crimes? So I'm talking about crimes against peace and security of mankind.

utterances.speaker: MS. TURKOVIC
utterances.text: First, I would like to address the first remark that you said that Mr. Smith and I are a little bit contradicting ourselves. I don't see that we are making any contradictory statements. Mr. Smith said that the Statute has to be interpreted, so whatever we find in the Statute has to be interpreted in light of the customary International Law and this is exactly what I said, you know, Article 7 has to be interpreted in the light of the customary International Law. Then you see people who are dealing -- I don't want to go into it, actually, but criminal law has lots of very specific theories that are very, very sophisticated, especially if you're going into the civil law, criminal law, existing in the civil law countries. It might be well that people are well versed in what crimes against peace are, what crimes against humanity are, not necessarily meaning that they really know in each detail that preparation is punishable, what aiding and abetting in Germany and in France and I don't know where means, and how to conciliate all of that. I know that all these crimes are very complicated and I believe that drafters of the Nuremberg Charter and the ICC Statue had that in mind, but anyhow did not draft these documents in terms that planning of war crimes or planning of crimes against, you know, whatever, is punishable, and I think that they had deeply thought about that, especially if we see that the language first was used in the ICC Statute and then it went out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We now move on to the motions in relation to the form of the indictment, and I see Mr. Smith has kindly presented an agenda. Again, as far as who presents the argument is concerned, that's a matter for you, but what I invite you to do is to present all the Defence argument together and then we'll call upon the Prosecution. But before you do, there's one matter for Mr. Kovacic. There is a motion on behalf of your client asking for a bill of particulars in relation to the indictment, and I wondered whether you wanted to address us on that at some stage this afternoon, in which case this -- during the course of this argument it might be a suitable stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, yes, perhaps I could do that then, but Mr. Kordic's defence will also be referring to their motion regarding the vagueness of the indictment, and since my motion for a bill of particulars relates to the same area, perhaps we could share or, rather, divide that section into two parts when I could argue my motion for a bill of particulars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It might be most convenient then, when you decide you want to join in, just indicate or at the end, whichever, when the other defence advocates have finished, but it may be convenient to deal with it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) may I join in, if I may be permitted to choose, after colleague Geneson, then I should like to add on to his argument my own submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We will argue these motions in the following fashion: I will argue the multiple charging matter first, Mr. Geneson will argue the vagueness matter second, and Mr. Kovacic will join that argument. Then Mr. Geneson will argue the 73 motion, form number 3 after that, and then I will finish by arguing a motion number 4 and the failure to allege nexus to international armed conflict. We will rest on our briefs, as the schedule indicates, on form of the indictment motion number 5 dealing with the failure to plead under all elements under Article 2(d), and if I may put a chart up before I commence, Your Honour, and if I may ask that these materials be passed out, I have three copies for the tribunal and one for the Prosecutor I would appreciate it. Your Honour, motion for the form of the indictment number 1 deals with the Prosecutor's multiple charging of the same offences in the indictment. The remedy we request is that the indictment be dismissed as a whole, or in the alternative, that the Prosecutor be limited to charging under Article section -- Article 5 section (h) of the Tribunal Statute dealing with persecution, and then there are additional combinations of strikings of provisions in the indictment in various combinations laid out in our brief that result from the logic of the arguments, and if Your Honours agree with various parts of the arguments then you will necessarily, I think, come to the conclusion that the reliefs requested there are appropriate. Let me start then by saying that criminal systems worldwide have developed rules against charging the same offence in multiple ways. They have done this because they have found multiple charging to be fundamentally unfair. There are, and we have referred to them in our briefs, common-law concepts of multiplicity and lesser included offence. There are civil law concepts of imperfect concurrence, and the three types we have outlined in our brief. The policies which lay behind these provisions and which have driven their development by judges over the years are also set out in our brief, and they involve, first, justice, the protecting the accused from the obvious prejudice that we have articulated there of defending against multiple charges for the same offence. Secondly, a prevention of the abuse and discretion by Prosecutors, Prosecutors when charging have a tremendous scope of power available at their fingertips and the Court is the proper vehicle and the proper institution for ensuring that the Prosecutor pleads wisely and properly under the rules, time honoured traditional rules that have been developed around the world. And thirdly, a judicial economy and efficiency, again in this case we are faced with both Your Honours and the Defence a multiplicity of Counts, each having separate elements, each having various villages, various locations, and all of the elements of every Count at every location have got to be proved by the Prosecutor the way he has pled the case beyond a reasonable doubt before a conviction can take place on any one. And we have indicated in our brief the ways in which you can have difficulties sorting out what has actually been proven when faced with a massive matrix of this sort. And the Defence, of course, has to defend every point. Let me then establish the fact that there is multiple charging here. And I urge Your Honours, lest there be any doubt, to see how it is illustrated first 5 (h), as we have argued, overlaps and is charged through paragraph 37 of the amended indictment, overlaps every other charge, counts 1 and 2 overlap every other charge in the indictment. And we have demonstrated that on Table 1 to our brief, and it is further demonstrated in this chart that I have put up in front of Your Honours. The left-hand side of the chart, which I'm sure you can't read from that distance, shows the elements of paragraph 37 which lays out the components of the persecution charge. And each one is given a different colour. As you will see then, in the paragraphs charging all of the other indictments, and they are laid out to the right, each one of those elements of the charge of persecution under 5 (h) is re-charged effectively under one of the other -- one or more of the other indictments, and the colour matching indicates it, and so that you can read it. I have given you a handout which for each color shows you the paragraph under 37 and then shows you where in each other part of the Count, each other Count that matter is double, sometimes triple charged. Secondly, in addition to the 5 (h) and everything else overlap, there is overlap as we have indicated in our brief among and between Articles -- charging under Articles 2, 3 and 5. That will be obvious when you look at the amended complaint, because you will have one description and then you will have, essentially, the same acts charged under both Article 2 and Article 3 or whatever. Those relationships are illustrated in Table 2 to our brief. So having dealt with the question of whether there is multiple charging, let you us now go to the question again of: Is this Trial Chamber free to consider this issue? The answer, I believe, is: Yes. There is no Appeals Chamber decision on the rules involving multiple charging. There is a Kupreskic decision, which we believe and our brief supports our view of the overlapping and improper multiple charging. Under that Kupreskic case the Prosecutor has the burden of proof. That's important to remember. The Prosecutor has the burden of proof to show that as to each offence, potentially multiply charged there are both differed elements and different interests. And when you look at the Prosecutor's reply brief, I think you will see that while they say there are both different elements and different interests, when you examine the interests carefully, they are generally a restatement of one of the elements as a practical matter. Now, let me summarise by saying it is the Defence's assertion that this is essentially a Section 5 (h) case as charged. By "as charged" I mean when you look at paragraph 37, which is then re-charged in all of the other Counts, so that they start with paragraph 37, and the sense that they have that there was a campaign of persecution and then they list the components, and then they double charge all the components once they have listed them, and it doesn't purport to be including but not excluding others. That list in paragraph 37 says here it is. Here's what we think persecution consists of in this case. So, in short, as charged, this is a 5 (h) case, and then they simply added everything else on in overlays of charging. We believe that, as I indicated, this results in a massive matrix, that this Court and the Defence is faced with dealing with. We believe that in effect this case has been radically overcomplicated. This is a 5 (h) case. All of the indictment, except 5 (h), should be stricken. It's all duplicative. This is fairer to the defendant, it is easier for the Court. And, finally, the Prosecutor can put in every bit of evidence that he wants to put in in the 5 (h) charge, because that charge, the elements of that charge are what overlap in all of the other cases, all of the other Counts. So it's all in his 5 (h) charge. And he can make his case there. If it turns out that he cannot prove, as we believe he will not be able to, a 5 (h) case, then he may at that time, as is traditionally done in the common law and under the relevant doctrines in the civil law, assert that he has, however, proved certain things that are lesser included offences. In that way we do not all deal with all of the matrix, we deal with the real case and we deal with any additional elements to be independently argued if the Prosecutor proves them, and if he is not able, as we think he will not be able to do, to make out a 5 (h) case of persecution. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, I have two questions. The first, you say that the Kupreskic test calls for different interests and different elements, and I think you made a point that they are cumulative, but you argue that if one looks at the indictment, the interests are a mere restatement of one of the elements. I would like you to illustrate that. Secondly, you didn't refer to the rule under the Tribunal, the Akayesu case, which sets up roughly the same kind of test as Kupreskic, but in the alternative. Would you like to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Let me take the last one first, as I am still looking to find you a good illustration on your first point, Your Honour. We believe, for the reasons we have stated in our brief, that the Akayesu test is not consistent with the law relating to common law and civil law on this point by allowing either the one or the other to be different. It is an outlyer, if you like, as to the present law and the perceived wisdom on these matters. And the third element in the Akayesu test, to allow the Prosecutor to describe the conduct as a reason or making a charge seems to us wholly inappropriate. Maybe the best word to use. I can either try to take a moment now and find you an example or Mr. Geneson can argue and I can come back to it, whichever Your Honours prefer. It's a matter of focusing on the right part of the brief, looking at the right sentence and finding the right illustration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am quite satisfied to have you come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Geneson.

utterances.speaker: MR. GENESON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I am going to do my best to not retread the same ground that we have enumerated in our filings, but I think it's important to remind the Tribunal that the Secretary-General's report prohibits charging based on mere association. Contrary to the position the Prosecutor has taken, the Nuremburg Tribunal is not the basis for the law of this Tribunal and mere membership and association in a political party is not a vehicle through charging. There is in fact individual liability, and that's what the Secretary-General's report speaks to. The indictment in its current form essentially lays out what one could describe as status charging. In paragraphs 24, 25, 26, 27, I may be wrong on one of those, but I believe it is in that group of paragraphs, there is a pejorative description of a certain political organisation in Bosnia with an explication that the defendant, Kordic, was a member and a senior officer in that organisation over a period of time. Later in the indictment various generic descriptions of bad conduct are enumerated. The basis for all the intervening charges are a crossover of some generic bad conduct and membership or relation to that organisation. That is impermissible on its face. But, worse, the actual charging language provides no concise, specific statement of facts upon which the defendant can defend himself. Let me note specifically, and I'll pick Count 7 through 13, the charging language. I would note that, as explained by Dr. Turkovic, and as agreed to by the Prosecutor, I suspect they will not disagree that each one of the itemised, alleged violative language here are "ors," they are not conjunctive. The Prosecution, I suggest would never claim that it has to prove all these things conjunctively, so I'll add the word "or" just to make it clear and for emphasis. But tracking paragraph 42, we have from about January, 1993 to approximately October, 1993, that's a ten-month period, Dario Kordic, together with, and I want to emphasise that language, together with members of the HCHB or the HRHB or the HVO and/or their leaders or armed forces or agents, caused or planned or instigated or ordered or committed or aided and abetted the planning or the preparation or the execution of murders or wilful killings or the wilful causing and infliction of serious injury or great suffering to body and health or physical or mental suffering or inhumane acts, or inhumane treatment upon and against a generic group called Bosnian Muslims in the following 12 towns. I would suggest, Your Honour, that based on that charging language no one in this courtroom, except maybe the Prosecution, knows who the victim or the victim was, victims or victim was, just a generic group, whether they were killed, whether they were seriously injured, whether they suffered greatly, whether they had physical or mental, inhumane treatment inflicted on them, or what kind of treatment. Where those particular events happened, again, we don't know, except maybe in one of 12 towns, when during that ten-month period they happened, who caused it, who instigated it, who ordered it, who committed it, or who aided and abetted it. Within a range of, if you look at the description of the people involved, maybe thousands of people, because it includes armed forces and agents. How it was done and other than the fact that Dario Kordic was together with one or more of these people, unnamed people, in this same organisation or organisations. How Dario Kordic was involved in any of these acts, it is pure status charging. We don't know what the crime was, except in a very generic, unspecified way. We don't know who was hurt, how they were hurt, by whom they were hurt, but Dario Kordic was together with the violator. Now, if you look at the indictment, it's very plain what's missing, and that's that concise statement of specific facts as to what happened. When I first appeared before this Tribunal about a month ago, I mentioned something. I'll just repeat it again, not to belabour the point. Mr. Scott and I come from a similar background. We used to be U.S. Federal Prosecutors for many years, so I can say that I have drafted hundreds of indictments and probably reviewed many more for other young Prosecutors. And when I read this, there is something that's very, very obvious. It sort of leaps out what's missing. That's what we call the "to wit" clause or the "in that" clause if you don't like the term "to wit." And what that means, very, very specifically, is that concise statement of fact. When you charge an individual in a criminal indictment, you say that on or about such and such a date John Doe --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GENESON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. On or about such and such a date, John Doe violated a statute by causing, aiding and abetting, instigating specific criminal conduct, and then you say: To wit, John Doe did on such and such a day cause the following people or people to, for example, go get five pounds of plastic explosive from the stocks at this location, go to that town and blow up that building. So the defendant knows what it is that he supposedly did. Else he can't answer the charges. That's what's missing from all these charges. We have an allegedly bad organisation, in fact just a political organisation, generic bad events, and then a crossover, together with some unknown, undefined massive potential group of people. Dario Kordic somehow is related to those events, with no specificity. I would just mention one other issue that arose in the pleadings that the Prosecution was kind enough to respond to, and that has to do with the definition of persecution. The Prosecution seems to suggest that it can take persecution and expand it around any law that was discriminatory in nature, just because there was a conflict. I would suggest the Court and the Prosecution is quite familiar with many laws that are discriminatory in nature. Most malum prohibitum laws are that. An example -- and an extreme example, but one that's typical -- is in the U.S., and in many other countries, airline pilots are prohibited from being commercial airline pilots after the age of 60. Undoubtedly many of them are very skilled and probably have 30 years' experience, and shouldn't be prevented from continuing to be the captains of 747s. But they are; that's a law. To use an extreme example, if you took the Prosecution's view of the world, should there be a conflict in which the U.S. is involved, arguably, senior airline pilots who are over 60 are a protected class who are being discriminated against. A remarkable suggestion. Now, what is the reality of this? The International Criminal Court Conference this summer basically laid it out: There is no predicate for just any discriminatory law or regulation being the basis of persecution; it must be tied to other criminal acts which are specifically prohibited under international criminal law. Not what the Prosecution says, but it must be tied -- you cannot create a generic environment of any discriminatory law becomes a vehicle for a persecution charge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Geneson. We'll adjourn now. We'll continue -- perhaps, Mr. Kovacevic, you would like to begin at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, I will try to be brief. We are very short of time. First of all, I would like to say that as regards the vagueness of the indictment, I agree with what my colleague has said. Our standpoints are very similar, so I think I can shorten what I was planning to say. But I would like to draw attention to some points. First of all, if we look at the sources of the law or what we may set up for ourselves as the sources, we have to bear in mind three things. The first of these is that one of the fundamental principles in all penal procedures, in all national jurisdictions is that the accused has the right to be informed in detail of the relative elements of the indictment, and by this the legislators usually specify time, place, victims, perpetrators or the role of the accused in the commission of crimes. This is the foundation which all of us always have in mind, and we know that we must have indictments which have to contain information about these elements, otherwise we do not know what we are defending against. Of course, I need not underline that the ICTY Statute in Articles 21, 24(a) and 18(4) has adopted this principle consistently, and this is quite precise and quite clear. And it says quite clearly that the accused has to be informed immediately and in detail of the nature and the causes of the charges alleged against him. The indictment has to contain a precise statement of facts and of the crimes with which the accused is charged and so on and so forth. So the question is how these criteria are to be interpreted in practice, and how the definitions are approached by various people. This is all stated in the submission and the definitions in the International Convention on Human and Civil Rights, and the European Convention on Civil Rights are also very precise and have provisions on the preciseness of the indictment and the details that the accused has a right to be informed of through the indictment. I think that this indictment has a number of omissions, and in my opinion it reduces to a considerable extent the possibility of preparing a relevant and valid defence by the accused, not the least because the indictment, in most of the counts, is so broad and it refers to a very long period of time, so that the Defence has to deal with an enormous number of details which are not always important in order to understand what the indictment is referring to or perhaps not referring to in a certain count. I think this puts the Defence in a position where it is forced a priori to deal with a very broad range of facts, and when the Prosecution presents its case, then we may find that they are, in fact, referring to something else. So I will not repeat what is written in the submission, but in the indictment we should be given more details. First, about the factual basis of each particular count of the indictment. Then we should be given more details which will clarify the time -- the time of the acts alleged against the accused. I need not reiterate that my client is being charged with acts over a period from April 1992 until the end of September 1994, and we are talking about a very turbulent time in which many events took place, so that every count which is so broad as to time is not clear and makes us have to deal with things which may not be relevant. Furthermore, in any case, I think we should get at least the minimum information about who the victims are, because most often we do not know whether the victims were civilians or soldiers, and this, of course, changes the legal nature of a case, because if the victims were soldiers we cannot talk about the crimes being alleged. What seems especially important to me, but it has already been referred to in other submissions today, and that is the role of the accused in the acts committed. What form of activity is the accused being charged with? Along with this, with the role, I think that certain improvements should be made in the indictment to make it clear, because the mens rea is not clear in the counts alleged. Then the participants should be specified, because it says that "Mario Cerkez, together with members of..." and so on, "With their leaders, agents..." and so on, who were these agents? With whom did Mario Cerkez act? They should be identified and so on. That is why I move and request that the Court should tell the Prosecution to specify the indictment in all parts where this is necessary, so that the indictment can be fully understood and so that the Defence can be prepared with reference to specific acts, specific places, a specific time and a specific role by the accused and not as a broad defence which may not be very precise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Geneson again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might answer the Judge's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Should I do that at this point or wait until--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do that now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I refer you to paragraphs 10 and 11 of the Prosecutor's response to our motion on the form of the indictment number 1, and in particular two examples. The last sentence of each of those paragraphs, the last sentence of paragraph 10 speaking of Article 2, grave breaches, says, "These prohibitions aim to criminalise certain conduct," and I take the word "aim" to mean an assertion to interest or value, although it's not clearly stated, "Aim to criminalise certain conduct during inter-state particularly in respect of protected persons." "Protected persons" is an element of the crime, the fallen into the hands of the adversary. So you have a mixing of one use, articulation of interest in terms of the element. Also in the last paragraph of -- sentence of paragraph 11, it says, "In respect of Common Article 3," and they're speaking now of Article 3 of the Statute, "In respect of Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions in particular, these rules promote the protection of all persons no longer taking part in hostilities." Now, I take the word "promote the protection" to be a statement about interest. They then go on to say, "The protection of persons not or no longer taking part in hostilities." That's an element. "Whether international or internal, from the most serious forms of inhuman treatment, including violence to life and torture," that's a direct reference to the various crimes and their elements. So I think it can be established that they have not borne the burden of making a clear and persuasive argument on interests and elements but particularly interests with regard to the various sections of the Statute. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could that not be because there is a level at which the concept of elements and the concept of interests overlap?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think it could be, Your Honour, but the test articulated in Kupreskic turns on interests on the one hand and elements on the other. If I were articulating the relevant interest, I would say that all of the provisions of the Tribunal Statute have the same interest, and that interest is that articulated by Michael Boch in the International Encyclopedia of Law where he says that International Humanitarian Law is designed to "Preserve civilisation and humanity during war." I think all of these provisions have essentially the same interest and it shades into the elements, the elements tend to be more differently articulated, but the test requires both a different interest and different elements or that they should not be double charging, Your Honour. That's our argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. GENESON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Let me address Article 7 and the 7(1), 7(3) issue. The Defence recognises that a number of Chambers have dealt with this issue, but we're asking this Chamber to look at it afresh. I guess the starting point of the argument really goes to Protocol 1 of the Geneva Convention, Article 86, which is the underpinnings for these exclusionary statements, that is the statements which prohibit the use of certain defences. Let me just quote from Article 86. "The fact that a breach of the conventions or of this Protocol was committed by a subordinate does not absolve his superiors from penal or disciplinary responsibility as the case may be if they knew or had information which should have enabled them to conclude, in the circumstances at the time, that he was committing or was going to commit such a breach, and if they did not take all feasible measures within their power to prevent or repress the breach." From that flows this language. If you look at Article 7, it almost cries out for a slightly different layout of the printing. The first section, 7(1), is the vehicle by which the Prosecutor charges individuals. It's, in effect, the tube through which it's all drawn. But (2), (3) and (4), in reality, should probably be tabbed over one notch with the heading "on available defences." In each one there is language to the effect that shall not relieve such person of criminal responsibility, does not relieve his superior of criminal responsibility, and shall not relieve him of criminal responsibility, each tied to a senior person not being able to avoid criminal responsibility, in effect assert a defence predicated by an attenuated position from the actual violation. The Prosecutor suggests that you can charge under 7(1) and 7(3), in effect turns the defence or the defence unavailable into a vehicle for charging. We would suggest that that is only available if your indictment is vague enough. If it lacks the specificity of actually a direct charge, that is an individual either committed, instigated or aided and abetted an act, or an individual was liable for failing to prevent his subordinate, charged under 7(1), for committing, instigating or aiding and abetting in an act. In effect, even if you were to charge an individual as a perpetrator and also a director of his subordinate --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GENESON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I forget. -- and a director of his subordinate in the same act simultaneously, their violation would merge into one under 7(1). Hypothetically, you can even have a failure of the Prosecution for the senior person is a committer and a conviction of the subordinate as the committer and the senior person would be liable once again under 7(1), because you could not successfully defend by showing that he had been inadequate in his activity in terms of preventing the conduct, in effect, aiding and abetting, what one might even call an accessory before the fact. We would suggest that the tribunal look closely at the construction of Article 7 and look at the underpinnings, because, in fact, only the vague kind of generic charging that the Prosecutor is engaged in here permits them to claim that 7(3) is a stand-alone vehicle for Prosecution and not one of the three enumerated unavailable defences for senior personnel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will address the nexus question raised in motion number 4 in the form of the indictment. The Prosecutor must do more than simply prove, allege and prove that there is an international armed conflict, as he attempts to do -- she attempts to do. She must also allege and prove that there is a nexus between the matter charged and the international armed conflict, and in this regard I refer Your Honours to the law that is beginning to be articulated by various Trial Chambers and the Appeals Chamber. The Tadic Appeal Chamber notes: That the crimes must be "closely related" to allege to the alleged hostilities. The Tadic judgment says that "a sufficient nexus must be established." In the Furundzija judgment the Trial Chamber has said -- the question is "whether a nexus exists," and whether there is "an obvious link between the crime and the hostilities." The question of which hostilities, then, the Prosecutor is talking about and alleging and attempting to prove is a critical one, because there can't be an obvious link unless it is obvious what hostility the Prosecutor is talking about. And in this matter it is not simple in the former Yugoslavia, as the Tadic case has articulated. As they said in the jurisdictional decision, the "conflicts in the former Yugoslavia" can be characterised as "both internal and international or, alternatively, as an internal conflict alongside an international one or as an internal conflict that had become internationalised because of external support or as an international conflict that had subsequently been replaced by one or more internal conflicts or some combination thereof." The Prosecution in its response says, "We did allege that there was a nexus to a conflict." It is the Defence's argument, Your Honours, that something more is needed than the simple, flat assertion that there is a nexus to a conflict. Precise details are not necessary. The Prosecution goes on at some length about how this is very complex, they don't have to lay out all the precise details now. There is an undistributed middle, Your Honours, between, on the one hand, this very spare assertion of a nexus to a conflict and a wealth of detail that will come in at trial, and the Defence is arguing that much more, but not the wealth of detail, can be provided and must be provided as a matter of fair notice to the Defence. The Prosecutor has also argued that the legal standard applicable here can be left until trial, but, Your Honour, the question of whether a proper nexus -- what a proper nexus is and whether it is pled is a pure question of law. The question the Prosecution discusses in attempting to postpone Your Honours' consideration of this matter is the underlying question of whether there was or was not an international armed conflict. That requires facts. That will have to be dealt with at trial, but the pleading question, the question of the adequacy of the nexus is a question of law under the guidance from other Trial Chambers that I have just outlined and needs to be resolved at this time. Now, a critical problem with what the Prosecution says, if you look at paragraphs 8 or paragraphs 13 or paragraph 16 of their response, they simply assert that the HV, that is to say Croatian army troops, intervened and that there was an international armed conflict. They never specified whether the HV are said to have intervened in 1992 against the Serbs when it can be alleged that the HV troops came into Herzegovina, not Central Bosnia, in 1992 to assist the Muslims in the fight against the Serbs. They never specify whether that's what they mean by HVO intervention or whether they mean to allege that the HVO, which in the Defence's view, and we will show this at trial, was only -- whether the HV was only ever in Herzegovina, whether the HV in 1993 and '94 in the essentially separate internal conflict between the Bosnian Muslim community and the Bosnian Croat community, which subsequently broke out, whether they argue that the HV intervened in that conflict against the Muslims. Now, this is not a great level of detail, but it is critically important to what it is they are saying, and whether it is defensible and how the defence establishes its case. I invite Your Honours to look at paragraphs 8 and 13 and 16 and the specificity even at this level is simply not there. In conclusion, the Defence asserts that the Prosecutor cannot show, not only has not, cannot show a nexus to support the indictment pre-May of 1993, because the HV, if it was in -- if it were in Bosnia at all, was in Herzegovina, intervened in 1992 against the Serbs on behalf of the Muslims and under an agreement between Croatia and Bosnia.
