We assert that they also do show no nexus between the HV and the HVO in Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993, which is the time period during which there was a conflict, an internal conflict, between the Muslim community and the Croat community in Bosnia, but even there, even if they were to show a nexus to the HV and Herzegovina during that time period, and against that opponent, that is to say the Muslims, Herzegovina, Western Herzegovina is a very different location than the Central Bosnian region, the Lasva Valley region where there is a conflict that this case turns on the resolution of. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Perhaps we can have your chart down. Take the easel down. Could we have the easel down, please. Mr. Smith, I don't know if you could reduce that chart for the Trial Chamber. It looked a useful production.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can leave this version and then I have got a second version that deals just with Mr. Cerkez, because of course the Counts differ as between the two. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would be helpful. There is no need to leave one, but if you could get one in reduced size, that would be useful. Thank you. Yes, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would it be convenient if I dealt both with vagueness and with nexus and then Mr. Dixon can deal with the two outstanding matters rather than taking them in the precise order. And in each case I think I can be comparatively brief and very brief. The forms of indictment with which this Tribunal is familiar, and we will become familiar, may differ significantly from the forms of indictment which we have all been accustomed in other jurisdictions. A theme of indictments elsewhere is that they sometimes can be very brief indeed and far less clear in the allegations that they are made -- making them. For example, this indictment is, which the Court will see, contains preamble almost by way of general allegations and background, which explain how it is that the defendants' conduct is alleged to fit into an overall scheme of thing and thus indeed to become criminal. So the general assertion that the defendants are undersupplied with detail because the indictment is in some way short on detail simply isn't correct. They are very full indictments. And, of course, they are now the conventional form of indictment within this Tribunal. Turning to their detailed problems that my learned friends raised with you. In each case, of course, you are dealing with people somewhere up the pyramid or triangle of responsibility. And as is clear as a matter of logic, and indeed covered by authority, as set out in our pleading, the further up that triangle or pyramid you go, the less likely is it that complete specificity in relation to any particular crime on the ground may be alleged. For, of course, people at the top in command may have created successfully by intention or otherwise a distance between themselves and the range of offences for which they may be proved to be responsible. You will, I trust, remember the -- or be able to remind yourself of what is said in paragraph 25 of our response on this particular motion. We say that so far as both of these defendants are concerned, the provisions of Article 18(1) and Rule 47(b) have indeed been complied with. It's not a detailed narrative that's required, but a concise statement of facts and of the crimes with which the defendant is charged that has to be set out. They are indeed on full notice of what is alleged against them, not only from the particular setting out of the Counts with which they are charged, but by reason of all the preceding material which sets out, for example, in Mr. Kordic's case, the bodies of which he was an officer and how it was that in those positions he was able to do this and that. We would invite Your Honours to say that there is absolutely nothing in the argument that this indictment is either out of the ordinary in any sense for this Tribunal or inappropriate to the facts that it is clear and on notice these defendants have to face. And because we are not going to repeat what is set out in our motions, we'll leave it there, subject to any questions that you may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE

As to number 8 or, I beg your pardon, the indictment motion 4, because of nexus, again we've addressed this fully in our response. This is a matter of evidence, is it not, again, the allegation of international armed conflict and the nexus is made and it will be for the evidence to establish whether it is made or not. Now is not the time to be deliberating upon it or striking it out. As with the previous general concern that Your Honours raised and expressed, this will be -- it's all set out to some degree in the indictment, but it will be more particularly addressed in any event at the stage of the Pre-Trial brief. They are certainly on notice under Article 2, international armed conflict, and Article 3, where armed conflict is sufficient, and we've named the various bodies that it is said are involved within the general part of the indictment. So that this is again, in a sense, perhaps premature. It's a matter of evidence and there is no way it can be taken further simply on the pleading, the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect to the motion on cumulative charging, we submit that we are justified in cumulative charging in this indictment for a number of reasons. Firstly, the Tribunal is empowered to charge all violations, that's in Article 1 of the statute of International Humanitarian Law, and then under the particular Articles that follow the rules under International Humanitarian Law are set out in detail. Secondly, there is no prejudice, we would argue, to the accused for being charged with different offences for the same conduct. The matter can be sorted out at the sentencing stage and the accused need not serve a double penalty for being convicted of more than one offence for the same conduct. Thirdly, the offences charged in the indictment are different offences with different histories; they've got different elements, and they protect different interests as well. For example, Article 2 applies only to offences that are committed during international armed conflict and only to persons who are protected specifically by the Geneva Conventions, whereas Common Article 3 applies to all persons who are not involved in hostilities during any conflict, whether that be international or internal. To the extent that there might be an overlap between articles 2 and 3, we believe it's justified nevertheless to have both charges, because it is only under Article 2 that a record, if it's found, can be made that an international armed conflict existed, and that the persons who are protected persons in terms of the conventions, that they fell within one of the categories, such as being prisoners of war. Fourthly, there is also no recognised system of lesser included offences within the Statute Rules or the jurisprudence of the Tribunal at this point, and therefore it's necessary to charge all the offences that cover the conduct. All of the Trial Chambers to date, both Trial Chambers in the Rwanda Tribunal and in this Tribunal, have adopted the approach of permitting cumulative charging, as I've outlined; that's Trial Chambers in the Tadic, the Blaskic, and the Kupreskic cases, for example, and we would invite Your Honours to follow this jurisprudence in permitting cumulative charging. Finally, in respect of persecution, we wish to submit that the acts of persecution themselves can be charged as other crimes against humanity. We would say that these acts constitute different crimes with different elements, and they protect different interests. Persecution as a crime can encompass many acts: Acts which are judicial, economic, physical, which deprive civilians of one of their basic or fundamental rights, whereas the other crimes against humanity, like murder or rape, are focused only on those crimes, and the elements and interests are confined to those crimes as well. So it's for these reasons that we would submit that the Defence motion should be rejected on the cumulative charging. I'll move on, if it pleases Your Honours, to the motion on Article 7(3). Briefly, we submit that superior responsibility is clearly recognised as an independent and separate form of individual criminal responsibility under international humanitarian law. There is no need to, as the Defence has suggested, first prove that the perpetrator either ordered or instigated or committed one of the offences before Article 7(3) is applicable. If a superior either knew or should have known that offences were being committed by his subordinates and he failed to prevent or punish those acts, that alone is a basis under international humanitarian law, to attract criminal responsibility. We have in our brief listed the numerous authorities that support this point, including cases from the Second World War, the additional protocols, and decisions of the tribunals, the Celebici and Akayesu decisions, for example. We also wish to submit that it is permissible to charge Article 7(1) and 7(3) cumulatively, for a number of reasons. Firstly, the act involved can involve both forms of responsibility. For example, in a series of generally planned attacks, it is possible if an individual planned one or some of those attacks to charge that person for those attacks under Article 7(1); and also, at the same time, where he did not plan any of the other attacks specifically, charge him for preventing -- for failing to prevent or punish other attacks, providing it can be shown that he knew or should have known that those attacks were occurring. Secondly, there is no prejudice, we would submit, to the accused, because as submitted earlier, this matter can be sorted out on sentencing. Thirdly, Articles 7(1) and 7(3) are different forms of responsibility which should be recognised publicly in the record, if that constitutes the acts that the accused committed. And the full spectrum of the accused's conduct should be reflected in the judgment. Trial Chambers of both tribunals have supported cumulative charging of articles 7(1) and 7(3); for example, in the Blaskic and Celebici cases. And in the Celebici case specifically, one of the accused, Mr. Mucic, was held responsible for both participating in maintaining the inhumane conditions in the Celebici camp, and also for failing to prevent the acts that occurred within the camp. A bench of the Appeals Chamber has also held that these forms of responsibility can be charged cumulatively, and we would invite the Trial Chamber to follow this line of jurisprudence that has developed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Smith; do you want to reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'll reply, Your Honour, quickly on motion number 1 and motion number 4. On motion number 1, the majority of the points covered in the argument are dealt with adequately in our brief. But on the question of developments at the time of penalty, I would make three points, Your Honour. First, we have outlined in our brief the policies that apply and cause prejudice to the defendant, at the time of charging and during trial, by multiple charging. These are not addressed when multiple charging is allowed at the outset and through the trial, by the cumulative or concurrent penalties at the time of sentencing. Second, concurrent penalties are of little aid to a defendant where life sentences are at stake. And third, I would urge Your Honours not to ignore the time-honoured rules that have developed about charging simply on the assertion that concurrent sentences will not be granted. Judges, in developing those rules over many, many years in all systems, have not found it satisfactory -- because of the kinds of policies about the defendant's rights before and during trial that we have cited -- have not found it satisfactory to simply allow multiple charging willy-nilly because concurrent sentences can be granted later. On the motion number 4, I would simply disagree with my learned colleague that this is just a matter of evidence. This is a matter of pleading. And we believe firmly, and have asserted and continue to assert, that on the nexus question, as elsewhere, when we've argued the vagueness point generally , there is simply an inadequate pleading at this stage. We've taken, of course, Your Honour's point about the Pre-Trial brief. Mr. Geneson, do you have anything further?

utterances.speaker: MR. GENESON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would only note one thing, and that's in regards to the vagueness motion. I believe the Tribunal, through Your Honour, has indicated at least an interest and a direction to the Prosecution to resolve some of those vagueness issues. We appreciate that. But I would like to make a note for the record that until the Prosecutor files its Pre-Trial brief, we are handicapped, and that that specificity that is expected by the Tribunal is unavailable to the Tribunal and to us. It doesn't matter what it's done like elsewhere. We're used to it here." Your Honour, I would suggest that's not a valid basis to prepare a vague and nonspecific pleading. It handicaps the Defence; it remains as a handicap to the Defence until the Pre-Trial brief is filed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Bennouna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My question is addressed to the representative of the Prosecutor regarding cumulative charges. The President has just expressed the feeling of the Trial Chamber regarding the necessity of specifying the charges in the Pre-trial brief. And you accepted that. My question is as follows: The cumulative charges, it's not just a question of precision; it's a question of approach. Either one believes that one has multiplied charges, as we see it here, by repeating the legal basis underlying those charges -- I'm referring to paragraph 40, 40 different counts -- as a function of a legal basis. Or, what seems to me to be much clearer, and we hope that that will be guidance for you, you are basing this on criminal conduct which was the criminal conduct or behaviour alleged that you are alleging the accused of having committed. And then for each of those acts, you would indicate what are the legal bases for criminalisation which justify criminal proceedings. Because in fact, the same criminal behaviour or act can be prosecuted in different ways, as we see under humanitarian law, and that is why we have this repetition, but which sometimes defends different values within different frameworks. So my question is whether, at the level of the Office of the Prosecutor, you realise what we expect of you in the Pre-trial conference or brief: That is, to show to the Trial Chamber which are the criminal acts that you wish to prosecute and which are the legal bases for those charges, and on the basis of which you have made those charges, so that the trial may proceed and for us to be able to better manage the proceedings within a framework that has to exist in all legal proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I answer your question, although Mr. Dixon was dealing with this particular motion and response. The answer to your question is yes, we do understand what you desire, and indeed we've had that in mind for some time in the way that we've been preparing documentation. utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith. Have you got some observation on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It's a related point, Your Honour, that I think may be of assistance to the Tribunal, and that is the Prosecution has said that the lesser included offence doctrine is not enshrined or recognised at this Tribunal at this point. But I would remind Your Honours that the Akayesu decision in the Rwanda Tribunal has expressly noted that lesser included offences cannot be charged at the outset, and thus I take it recognises that the concept exists, and it might be useful as a device, as I indicated earlier, the indictment would pare down lesser included offences later argued. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.text: Now may be convenient to deal with the motion in relation to compliance with the disclosure requirements. utterances.text: I was going to ask Mr. Scott to deal with this because he's been very much dealing with disclosure, but I'll just discuss it if you'll just give me a moment. I don't think there's anything else. Will you give me a minute while I check?

utterances.text: Yes. I'm reminded, Mr. Nice, of this: As to whether there are any other witnesses on whom you're going to rely and whose statements haven't been disclosed.

utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber's order, when it first came out, was a matter of some discussion, as I think your legal officer may have mentioned to you. utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me take the matters covered in that motion one by one and start with the supporting material. utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is no statement of facts in precisely the form of the original indictment, but the Court will, of course, understand that applications in respect of proposed indictments are accompanied by documents that go to the confirming Judge, a pleading or motion of some form, which may well contain materials similar to, probably did, but that's really by way of a forecast of any argument that may be addressed to the Judge if the Judge, when, in this case, she heard the matter decided she wanted such argument. It's true that when the original indictment was confirmed, and I'm afraid I can't tell you why, how, by what mechanism, a statement of facts generated was provided. I think that preceded the participation with all of us here in this Tribunal, and so I simply don't know how that came about, but there is no reason for the document that is served ex parte to be made available to the Defence. I haven't considered, I have to tell you, whether I would like to make that document available or like to withhold it, because I hadn't known this particular topic was going to be raised today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your position is, Mr. Nice, that all supporting material has been made available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, because that isn't supporting material, that's a document of argument to the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would respond that it seems to me the statement of facts provided with the original supporting material was provided only because it was part of the supporting material, and because the nature of the proceeding before the confirming Judge is ex parte, it would not have been provided unless it were supporting material. Indeed, it would have been improper. If there is another document by whatever name which now is in effect or has the same substantive content as a statement of fact, then it seems to me the Prosecutor has conceded that that is part of the supporting material and that that should be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, I would like to support this submission. I consider this to be a very serious issue. I do not quite recall, though I did not prepare for this discussion, but I do the not recall ever us having any dilemmas regarding the scope of the rights under 66. Whatever the Prosecutor gave to the Judge when asking for the indictment to be confirmed, or in this case the amended indictment, constitutes supporting material and we're entitled to having that material disclosed. It is not up to the Prosecutor to decide that, "I gave this to the Judge to help the Judge decide and I will give something else to the Defence." The supporting material, as far as I can see it, is a unified set of supporting documents with which the Prosecutor sports his submissions, his document, his indictment, and it emerges from the Rules that whatever he has given to the Judge has to be disclosed to the Defence, the only exception being those matters that have to do with the protection of the victims and witnesses. This is for the first time for me to hear such a point being made. He seems to imply that there are some additional papers that have not been disclosed to us. We are late with the discovery, late with exculpatory material, and now it appears that we also are due to receive more supporting material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you want to say something, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that topic, no. I would only be repeating myself. It's not part of the supporting materials, no, it isn't. There is one other topic that I ought to just mention, and that is that the President who was the Judge dealing with the amended indictment has raised an issue not about the materials that were presented to her but she's raised an issue, it's being dealt with and it will be dealt with swiftly. I simply say that. It may or may not involve some other document being served, but I'll simply have to await her decision on that which won't come for a few days yet, but it arises from her determination in relation to the amended indictment and it can't be disposed of for a day or so yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'm bound to say, Your Honour, that the Defence is simply mystified as to what this decision is and what relation it bears to our request, and we're ill-equipped to argue or deal with the matter because obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we need trouble you with it. It's clearly an ex parte matter. Let's move on to the next area which you want to raise, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The second area then is the prior statements of the accused. The Prosecutor has essentially taken the position that there are no prior statements of the accused because they've not interviewed the accused, and we have laid out at page 15 of our motion the scope of the prior statements that we believe we are entitled to have if they are within the possession of the Prosecutor, and they include all written transcripts, all video, audio tapes of the defendant's statements, press reports, written letters, notes, ledgers, orders in particular, other writings of the defendant, and I think that a ruling is in order on the scope question. If the Prosecutor has none of these items and is prepared to state for the record that they have none of these items, including orders and further videotapes that they have not turned over to us, and I should say they have voluntarily turned some videotapes over to us, then there may be no need for an order, but -- a ruling, but it seems to me unless the Prosecutor is prepared to take the position that nothing we have asked for is available to them or within their hands in the scope and nature in which we have asserted in the pleading, then there simply needs to be a disposition on the matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll ask Mr. Scott deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the court, and I apologise to Judge Robinson for having to look around the pole here, but the Prosecutor's position on this point, Your Honour, is that this is governed by the Trial Chamber's ruling in the Blaskic case on the 27th of January -- well, first by the 27th of January, 1997, and then actually the final order on that point being dated 15 July, 1998. In that ruling, the Trial Chamber there ruled that prior statements, and I'm quoting, "Must be understood to refer to all statements made by the accused during questioning in any type of judicial proceeding which may be in the possession of the Prosecutor, but only such statements." We have stated to the Defence and it is no surprise to them, in fact there was a letter just some weeks ago, that there are no such statements made to any law enforcement official, any court concerning this case, any police officer or investigator. We asked by letter for them to confirm if they knew of any such statements to the contrary and they indicated none to us. So it is our position that as construed by the Blaskic Trial Chamber, that are no such statements by the accused to turn over, and they apparently agree that there are no such statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may address that response. The Blaskic Trial Chamber's decisions referred to are a change of position by that Trial Chamber. We believe and have argued that the original position the Trial Chamber took is correct. We believe we are entitled to the material we have requested and we do not concede and say nothing one way or another about what sorts of materials the Prosecutor is speaking about which he may have in his possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, there is a duty to disclose any material they are going to rely on in the trial. There is a duty to disclose any exculpatory material. What else could you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe that if there were material that the Prosecutor had which is not exculpatory but has other information in it that we, in putting our case together, believe would be material and relevant, but is not in their judgment exculpatory, whether they choose to use it in their case or not, we believe under the language of the Rules that we have an entitlement to it and the matter is posed for Your Honours' disposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Anything else that you'd like to refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The third category of information that we requested under Rule 66 are prior statements of witnesses. We've been given a large number of prior statements. The matter of redaction, well-known, has been dealt with at length and is now provided for under orders. We have the material that was not redacted, that is to say where there were no redactions. We have statements which are redacted, but there is a date for us to be provided with the unredacted versions of those statements. The critical problem is one that I think was discussed between Your Honour and the Prosecution a few moments ago, and that is whether all of the witness statements for persons to be presented at trial have been presented, and I take the Prosecutor's answer to be no, that has not been done, and they do not plan on doing it until as late as the 11th of March at the Pre-Trial conference when they are to produce their witness list. It would be, I think, possible for them to overprovide, that is to say to provide statements of people that are likely to be used in the trial without having to wait for a final decision, because of course the Rules provide that as things can happen in a trial, if the witnesses change as things go forward, there is a provision in the Rule for notification. So it seems to me that they could provide those materials at this point. The particular concern I have is if there were just one or two further witness statements that we would get on the 11th of March, I would not have terribly great concern, but I can't tell how many there are, and that's very close to trial. If there were a larger number, a significant number of witness statements that we would not get until that time, that would be a matter of great concern to me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution have dealt with that, but perhaps you can assist by indicating, Mr. Nice, an answer to that last point, which is clearly material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whether there will be a limited number or a substantial number, I think there will be quite a substantial number. I think that's inevitable. And I know it isn't -- I mean, it simply isn't possible to make -- no, it isn't possible to make an interim decision. The thing has to be dealt with compendiously and it involves both information coming to us, which has to be put together, and it involves making decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that, of course, is right, but you will bear in mind that the trial date is the 12th of April, and there must be a reasonable time for the Defence to prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am bound to say that I am disturbed, given the already very large number of witness statements provided to us, both of residents in the valley and of persons outside the valley and subsequent conches of witness statements to find that there is still yet a very large volume beyond that that they cannot provide until that point. It will put the Defence in a very difficult position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution are on notice. And, of course, the Trial Chamber, it may be, will have to rule on what is relevant and what isn't. The trial must be within reasonable proportions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if that calls for any response by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But let me also just make one other point. As well as adding to what might be a sort of first step, mental witness list, there may also be subtractions from that number as well. With Your Honours' point in mind, after all, if any particular topic is potentially covered by many witnesses, then subject to it becoming clear in cross-examination that the particular topic is challenged or heavily challenged, we can probably deal with that topic with one or a couple of witnesses, and we would therefore remove either immediately from the witness list or at a later stage other people who could cover that topic. So it's not just addition, it's addition and subtraction, and quite a lot of the subtraction, I hope, will go on from the mental list, as it were, from the first idea of the list before we ever get to March the 11th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one last category of material raised in our motion, and that is the Rule 68 exculpatory material, and the Prosecution has said and taken the position that they have provided all of the exculpatory material available. I would simply reiterate the breadth of the rule in Rule 68 that the material tend to suggest or tend to mitigate guilt in any way. And at one point in the explanation by the Prosecutor as to steps they had gone through while they, understandably and properly, did not go into detail, nonetheless, it were the case that they -- given what they have given us, with just references to our client's name in testimony from other witnesses, if all they have done is a computer name search, I would submit, Your Honour, that that will not have turned up all the exculpatory material. And the Defence will be taking the position in trial, if material comes into the record that was attempted to be used or brought into the record that should have been disclosed as exculpatory by the Prosecutor, we will be reminding the Trial Chamber and the Prosecutor the breadth of this language and of the need for doing more than just a computer name search. That is the last matter covered in our motion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I take it that the Prosecution have in mind their duties under that Rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We certainly have our duties in mind. We have done considerably more than simply a computer name search. I also have in mind that when the Defence case is made clear by the service of their Pre-Trial brief, issues will become further identified and isolated, which may both free some topics from consideration as exculpatory and identify others. And we are not blind or deaf to the possibility that our work will have to be redirected, when the issues become clear. For the time, as I think the Chamber will know, we have responded to a very long letter from the Defence which, I think, identified some 28 -- something like 28 issues they said were capable of being exculpatory in nature. We replied to them, I think, to the effect not that we accepted they were accurate in their list of 28 categories, because we certainly neither accepted nor were prepared to be bound by that, but that we had read it and we had it in our mind when we were conducting any of our operations of reviewing material for its potential exculpatory effect. That's the appropriate way to deal with it, because, of course, the judgment about material being exculpatory, and it is a judgment, has in the first instance to be ours, with the possible potential for recourse ex parte to the Chamber on marginal matters should that ever become necessary. But it has to be our judgment. But we have been making our judgment with the Defence's extremely detailed suggestions in mind. We can do no better than that, in our respectful submission. JUDGE BENNOUNA (Interpretation): Mr. Nice, if I understood well what you are saying, you said that you respected the pertinent provisions of Article -- Rule 66 and 68, and that, therefore, there's no reason to go any further in terms of respect of provisions, Rule 66 and 68; is that what you are saying? In your judgement, for the moment, of course that's a judgement, especially regarding exculpatory material, you have respected the provisions and the obligations that you have under Rule 66 and 68? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I'll deal with it in this way. I think there are two parts. As to the entitlement to disclosure, it's our argument, as set out in the pleadings, that 66 and 68 identify exhaustively that to which the Defence are entitled. Sixty-eight, for exculpatory material, requires us to exercise a judgment. In order to exercise that judgment we have to look at whatever material we judge appropriate to look at. We've gone beyond, as I've said, a mere computer name search, and we have, we believed, applied a very generous test. Not a generous test, because -- that's an inappropriate term. A very wide test, we believe, in order to ensure that anything that could be judged exculpatory is turned over. I hope that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you want to add something, Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The Prosecutor is in fact correct, the Defence has tried to be helpful in the matter of Rule 68 by providing the Prosecutor with a list of material of questions and matters as to which we think material would be exculpatory. We are surprised that there is no more, given the volume of the material in this case and the breadth of Rule 68, but we are grateful to our learned colleagues for their efforts to review the material and provide us what they can and to discharge their duties, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's now half past five and we should adjourn unless there are any other urgent matters which anybody wants to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: None for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I take it none for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: None for the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 5.30 p.m., sine die. 24 25
